G01-CORE-BOUNDARY.name: No decision boundary enforcement

risk_score.rationale: High likelihood because most agentic deployments lack explicit rule layers; HIGH impact because every automated decision is ungoverned until fixed

evidenced_by: Client states system executes decisions automatically (intake C1=Yes)
No rule enforcement layer or decision policy documented (intake C2=No or Unsure)
No defined permitted/prohibited conditions for the AI's decisions
Agent output directly triggers action with no intermediate evaluation step
evidence_required: Documented ruleset defining permitted and prohibited decision conditions for each automated decision type
Version-controlled rule configuration file or policy document with named owner
Evidence of runtime enforcement — system logs showing rule evaluation occurring before action execution
Named individual accountable for ruleset maintenance with documented sign-off

healthcare.regulatory: DCB0160 (Health and Social Care Act 2012) mandates that all AI outputs affecting patient care must be reviewed by a qualified human before action is taken. An automated decision layer with no human review obligation is inconsistent with regulatory expectations. CQC inspections are increasingly citing the absence of this governance structure as a failure of safe care protocols.
healthcare.operational: Clinical AI decisions that execute without a rule boundary cannot be defended if they cause patient harm. The absence of an interception layer means clinical errors propagate directly — with no point at which a safety check could have caught them.
healthcare.reputational: A harmful clinical decision made by an ungoverned AI system, with no evidence of a control layer, is likely to be treated by CQC and NHS England as a systemic failure of patient safety governance — not an isolated incident.

financial_services.regulatory: FCA Principle 3 (management and control) requires firms to take reasonable care to organise and control their affairs responsibly. An AI system executing decisions with no rule enforcement layer cannot demonstrate that control. Under SM&CR, the named Senior Manager accountable for AI-influenced outcomes has no mechanism to evidence that governance existed.
financial_services.operational: Automated decisions that reach production without a rule evaluation layer cannot be unwound cleanly. Recovery depends on downstream complaint detection — by a customer, the FOS, or the FCA — at which point the harm has already occurred.
financial_services.reputational: An FCA enforcement action arising from an ungoverned automated decision — with no evidence of a control layer — is a public record. Consumer Duty requires firms to demonstrate they acted to deliver good outcomes. Absence of a boundary enforcement layer is direct evidence they did not.

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: The ICO's Recruitment Rewired report (31 March 2026) is unambiguous: many employers are already conducting solely automated decision-making in recruitment without acknowledging it. Under DUAA 2025 Articles 22A-22C, which came into force on 5 February 2026, an employer using ADM must be able to demonstrate that any human involvement in the process is genuine and meaningful — not a rubber stamp. The ICO defines the test precisely: the human reviewer must have real authority, discretion and competence to alter the decision before it is applied. A recruitment AI that filters, scores or rejects candidates with no rule enforcement layer has no mechanism to meet that test: without defined rules governing what the system can and cannot decide, there is nothing for a human reviewer to evaluate or override against. The DUAA's mandatory safeguards under Article 22C — right to be informed, right to make representations, right to human review, right to contest — all presuppose that the system's decision logic can be explained and bounded. No rule enforcement layer means none of these rights can be discharged. The ICO has confirmed enforcement action will follow for organisations that fall short; the absence of a decision boundary is the structural gap that makes every other safeguard unworkable.
sector_risk.legal: The SRA Code of Conduct for Firms requires effective governance structures and controls (Rule 2.1(a)) and identification and management of material risks (Rule 2.5). An AI system producing legal outputs — drafting, research, document review, advice summaries — with no rule enforcement layer cannot satisfy either obligation. The SRA has stated explicitly that COLPs are responsible for regulatory compliance when new technology is introduced (SRA Innovate: Compliance tips for solicitors). A rule enforcement layer is the structural mechanism by which a COLP can demonstrate that the firm's AI tools operate within defined, documented boundaries. Without it, the COLP has no evidence that the AI was governed — only that it was used. In 2025, the High Court sanctioned solicitors in both Ayinde v London Borough of Hackney and Gloriose Ndaryiyumvire v Birmingham City University for AI-assisted submissions that could not be verified. In both cases the underlying failure was the same: no defined boundary on what the AI was and was not permitted to produce for a given matter type. A rule enforcement layer is not a theoretical governance construct in this sector — it is the control that distinguishes defensible AI-assisted practice from the conduct those judgments condemned.
sector_risk.retail: Retailers deploying agentic AI — dynamic pricing engines, personalised promotion tools, automated stock replenishment, customer service bots — are making consequential consumer-facing decisions without a rule enforcement layer. The CMA's 2024 Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act and its AI principles for online platforms require that algorithmic pricing and personalisation tools operate within defined, auditable parameters. A dynamic pricing engine with no decision boundary cannot demonstrate compliance with CMA price transparency obligations. An automated customer service agent with no defined permitted/prohibited scope creates Consumer Rights Act 2015 exposure: any automated commitment made to a customer is binding, and an ungoverned agent has no mechanism to prevent out-of-scope commitments. ICO enforcement under UK GDPR Article 22 applies where automated decisions produce significant effects on consumers — including personalised pricing and credit-linked promotions — without a lawful basis or human review mechanism.

risk_full.regulatory: EU AI Act Art. 9 risk management obligation is not met. Where the system is classified high-risk, absence of a rule enforcement layer presents a direct compliance exposure.
risk_full.operational: Agent errors propagate directly to production with no interception point. Recovery depends on downstream detection — by a human, a customer, or a third party.
risk_full.reputational: No ability to demonstrate control post-incident. In the event of a harmful decision, the organisation cannot show that a governance layer existed.

G02-CORE-PROVENANCE.name: Provenance weakness

risk_score.rationale: HIGH likelihood because external data consumption without validation is the norm; MEDIUM impact because harm requires a downstream decision failure to materialise

evidenced_by: System consumes data from external or third-party sources (intake D1=Yes)
Data inputs cannot be traced back to a verified origin (intake D2=No or Unsure)
No validation step checks input data before it reaches the agent (intake D3=No)
Validation exists but is undocumented or inconsistently applied (intake D3a=No)
evidence_required: Data source register listing every external input to the AI system with origin, update frequency, owner and validation status
Validation procedure documentation or schema definitions applied to each external source before data reaches the agent
DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) covering AI system data inputs — mandatory where special category data is involved
Evidence of validation runs — logs, test reports or monitoring records showing validation is consistently applied

healthcare.regulatory: Patient data is special category data under UK GDPR Article 9. A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a legal requirement before any AI system processes patient records. Where inputs to the agent cannot be traced to a verified source, the ICO treats this as a data integrity failure. NHS AI governance policy requires that data feeding clinical AI is validated, owned, and auditable.
healthcare.operational: A clinical AI system acting on unverified or drifted patient data may produce a decision that causes direct patient harm. Without provenance documentation, root cause analysis after an incident is impossible — the organisation cannot show what data the agent received, when, or from where.
healthcare.reputational: An ICO investigation or CQC inspection following a patient safety incident will request evidence of data provenance controls. If none exist, the absence of a DPIA alone is a reportable breach — independent of whether harm occurred.

financial_services.regulatory: The Data Use and Access Act 2025 (DUAA 2025) establishes automated decision-making safeguards alongside FCA Consumer Duty obligations. Where an AI system makes or influences a credit, suitability, or advice decision using unverified data, the firm cannot demonstrate the data quality required under FCA Principle 2. UK GDPR Article 22 rights apply where automated decisions produce legal or similarly significant effects on individuals.
financial_services.operational: Credit decisions, suitability assessments, or claims outcomes produced from unverified inputs cannot be defended at the Financial Ombudsman Service. Without documented data provenance, the firm has no basis to reconstruct the decision or demonstrate it was made on accurate information.
financial_services.reputational: FCA enforcement actions increasingly reference data governance failures as evidence of systemic control weakness — not just technical error. A pattern of decisions made on unvalidated inputs is a Consumer Duty failure in its own right.

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: The ICO's 2024 audit of AI recruitment tools found that some tools were inferring protected characteristics — including gender and ethnicity — from candidate names rather than collecting that information directly. This is a data accuracy and fairness failure under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d). Under DUAA 2025 Article 22C, which came into force on 5 February 2026, employers relying on ADM must be able to discharge the candidate's right to contest a decision — which requires the employer to be able to identify the input data used and demonstrate it was accurate. Where inputs cannot be traced to a verified source, the right to contest is structurally unenforceable. The ICO's Recruitment Rewired report (March 2026) requires organisations to be able to explain both the logic and the data behind each automated decision. Without provenance controls, that explanation is impossible — and the employer's only defence to a discrimination claim is to produce records they do not have.
sector_risk.legal: Legal AI systems processing client data — case files, correspondence, precedent databases, statute repositories — are subject to UK GDPR accuracy requirements and SRA obligations on record integrity. Where AI outputs are based on unverified, drifted or third-party data sources that the firm cannot trace, the resulting advice or documents may be factually wrong. The SRA Code requires firms to maintain records demonstrating compliance (Rule 2.2); unverified AI inputs make that demonstration impossible. In Ayinde v London Borough of Hackney (May 2025), the court found that a barrister had relied on five fabricated case citations in submissions to court. The failure was not deliberate dishonesty — it was unverified AI input treated as reliable output. The court considered referral to the Bar Standards Board and warned that citing false authorities could amount to contempt of court. For law firms, provenance weakness is not a theoretical data risk — it is the precise failure mode that produced those outcomes. A firm that cannot trace every AI input used in client work to a verified source is structurally exposed to the same outcome on every AI-assisted matter it delivers.
sector_risk.retail: Retail AI systems — recommendation engines, demand forecasting, inventory replenishment — consume data from suppliers, third-party data brokers, loyalty platforms and external APIs. Where that data cannot be traced to a verified origin, the decisions it informs are compromised. A product recommendation engine acting on unverified supplier data may recommend discontinued, recalled or incorrectly priced products. A demand forecasting model consuming unvalidated external data may generate purchase orders that create financial and supply chain exposure. Under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d), personal data used in consumer-facing AI must be accurate — inaccurate inputs to a personalisation or targeting system are a data quality breach. Where consumer promotions or pricing are AI-generated from unverified data, CMA consumer protection obligations are directly engaged.

risk_full.regulatory: GDPR data integrity obligations and EU AI Act data governance requirements (Art. 10) apply where personal or sensitive data feeds the agent. Unverified inputs are a direct exposure.
risk_full.operational: Decisions based on unverified inputs cannot be reconstructed or defended post-incident. Root cause analysis becomes guesswork.
risk_full.reputational: Insurer exclusions are likely where data provenance is undocumented. Standard AI liability policies increasingly require evidence of input validation.

G03-CORE-AUDIT.name: Audit void

risk_score.rationale: HIGH likelihood because sealed audit infrastructure is rarely built alongside AI deployment; HIGH impact because absence of audit trail is itself a regulatory failure independent of underlying decision quality

evidenced_by: Decisions are not logged or only partially logged (intake E1=No)
No sealed, write-once audit trail exists (intake E2=No)
Organisation cannot produce a specific decision record on request (intake E3=No)
Logs exist but can be altered — not tamper-evident
evidence_required: Write-once decision log demonstrating every agent decision is recorded with timestamp, input summary, decision output and rule applied (if any)
Sealed audit trail mechanism — evidence that logs cannot be altered after creation (append-only storage, cryptographic hash, or equivalent)
Demonstrated ability to retrieve a specific decision record on request — test retrieval with sample date and decision ID
Retention policy for audit records aligned to applicable regulatory requirements (minimum 6 years for most regulated sectors)

healthcare.regulatory: DCB0160 requires a maintained hazard log and clinical safety case report as a legal condition of deploying any health IT system. These are contemporaneous records — they cannot be reconstructed after the fact. CQC inspections now routinely request DCB0160 documentation as evidence of safe care governance. Where no sealed record of AI decisions exists, the organisation cannot produce the clinical safety case the standard requires.
healthcare.operational: A patient safety incident involving an AI system with no decision audit trail leaves the organisation unable to determine what the agent decided, what data it received, or what rule it applied. Serious incident investigation and NHS England reporting all require this record. Without it, the investigation cannot proceed.
healthcare.reputational: The CQC's single assessment framework treats the absence of audit evidence as a governance failure in its own right. An NHS Trust that cannot produce a contemporaneous record of AI-influenced clinical decisions faces formal regulatory action — not just a recommendation.

financial_services.regulatory: The FCA has signalled that audit trail and explainability guidance will be formalised by end of 2026. Firms that cannot demonstrate a contemporaneous record of AI-influenced decisions are already in breach of FCA Principle 3 and operational resilience requirements. Under SM&CR, the named Senior Manager cannot demonstrate reasonable steps were taken if no decision record exists.
financial_services.operational: A Financial Ombudsman Service complaint about an automated credit, suitability, or claims decision requires the firm to produce a record of what decision was made, on what basis, and when. Without a sealed audit trail, the firm has no defence — and the FOS will find against it.
financial_services.reputational: An FCA enforcement action citing the absence of an audit trail is a public censure. It signals to the market, counterparties, and customers that the firm was operating AI systems it could not account for. That signal is not recoverable quickly.

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: DUAA 2025 Article 22C(3), in force since 5 February 2026, grants candidates the right to contest automated recruitment decisions. This right is structurally unenforceable if no contemporaneous record of the decision exists. The ICO's Recruitment Rewired report (March 2026) makes the record-keeping obligation explicit: employers using ADM must be able to explain how automated decisions were reached and why. The ICO's transparency obligations under UK GDPR Articles 13-15 further require employers to provide meaningful information about the logic involved in ADM and its likely consequences. None of these obligations can be discharged without a sealed record of each automated decision. At Employment Tribunal, the Equality Act 2010 section 136 reversed burden of proof means that once a claimant establishes a prima facie case of discrimination, the employer must produce evidence that no discrimination occurred. An employer with no decision record cannot discharge that burden — the absence of documentation is itself adverse evidence. The ICO has already contacted 16 organisations requiring improved practices; an audit void is the single gap most likely to be identified in any ICO engagement.
sector_risk.legal: The SRA Code of Conduct requires firms to maintain records demonstrating compliance with their obligations (Rule 2.2). Where AI is used to assist with client work — drafting, research, document review, advice summaries — and no record exists of what the AI produced and what human review was applied, the firm cannot demonstrate compliance. In Gloriose Ndaryiyumvire v Birmingham City University (2025), the court made a wasted costs order against a firm that had filed an application citing two fictitious AI-generated cases. The firm's position — that the AI document was a draft filed by administrative staff in error — failed because there was no audit record showing the document had been reviewed before submission. The court found the failures were improper, unreasonable and negligent. A sealed record of AI contributions — what was generated, when, by what tool, and what human review was applied — is the control that would have made that defence available. Without it, the firm had no basis to distinguish its supervised work from an unsupervised AI output. The SRA's risk outlook on AI identifies the absence of AI audit logs as the primary governance risk in the sector. This is the gap most likely to be the subject of a client complaint, a court intervention, or an SRA enquiry.
sector_risk.retail: A retailer operating agentic AI — automated promotions, dynamic pricing, chatbot commitments, personalised offers — with no sealed audit trail cannot defend any individual consumer interaction. Consumer Rights Act 2015 requires that any automated commitment made to a consumer is honourable: without a decision record, a retailer cannot confirm or deny what its AI system offered. CMA investigations increasingly request records of algorithmic pricing decisions for specific periods and product categories. Where no write-once log exists, the retailer has no response. ICO Subject Access Requests covering AI-driven marketing and personalisation require the organisation to produce records of automated decisions — including the data used and the decision output. Without a sealed audit trail, the SAR cannot be fulfilled.

risk_full.regulatory: FCA audit trail requirements and EU AI Act Art. 12 record-keeping obligations apply to automated systems making consequential decisions. Absence of a sealed audit trail is inconsistent with record-keeping obligations.
risk_full.operational: Root cause analysis after an incident is guesswork. Without a contemporaneous record, the organisation cannot identify what the agent decided, when, or why.
risk_full.reputational: Inability to produce an audit trail to a board, insurer, or regulator is itself a significant liability indicator — independent of whether the underlying decision was correct.

G04-CORE-ACCOUNTABILITY.name: Accountability gap

risk_score.rationale: HIGH likelihood because accountability structures are rarely formalised for AI systems; HIGH impact because personal liability for named individuals is unmitigated without this control

evidenced_by: No named individual is accountable for AI system decisions (intake F1=No or Unsure)
Accountable individual cannot intervene or override a decision in execution (intake F2=No)
No record of oversight actions taken — role exists but is not exercised (intake F3=No)
No defined escalation conditions triggering human review (intake F4=No)
evidence_required: Named individual formally designated as accountable for AI system decisions — documented in role description or governance charter
Override mechanism documentation — how the accountable individual can stop, modify or reverse a decision, and under what conditions
Oversight log or review record showing the accountable individual has actively exercised oversight — not just that the role exists
Escalation procedure defining conditions under which decisions are routed to human review before execution

healthcare.regulatory: DCB0160 requires that a named, qualified Clinical Safety Officer (CSO) is appointed and accountable for every AI system deployed in a clinical setting. This is a legal requirement under the Health and Social Care Act 2012 — not a best practice recommendation. Where no CSO is named and no override mechanism exists, the organisation is in likely to be challenged as a breach. CQC inspection failure for this gap results in formal regulatory action against the Trust or practice.
healthcare.operational: NHS AI governance policy is explicit: all AI outputs must be reviewed by a human before action is taken. Where no override mechanism exists, the named CSO cannot fulfil their legal duty. In the event of patient harm, personal professional liability is unmitigated — the accountable clinician cannot demonstrate they were in control.
healthcare.reputational: A serious patient safety incident involving an AI system with no named accountable clinician and no override record is likely to be treated as a systemic governance failure by CQC, NHS England, and the coroner if death is involved. The absence of a CSO is the headline — not the underlying decision.

financial_services.regulatory: SM&CR is unambiguous: accountability for AI-influenced regulated outcomes must sit with a named Senior Manager. This cannot be delegated to the technology. The FCA and PRA concluded that existing SM&CR structures are sufficient to cover AI — which means the accountability obligation already exists and is already enforceable. Where no named individual owns AI outcomes and no override mechanism exists, the firm has no SM&CR compliance for that system.
financial_services.operational: When an AI system produces a poor consumer outcome — a mis-sold product, an incorrect credit decision, a harmful automated communication — the FCA will ask which Senior Manager was accountable and what oversight they exercised. If the answer is no named individual and no override record, personal enforcement action against that individual is the likely outcome.
financial_services.reputational: SM&CR enforcement is public. A named individual cited for failure to oversee an AI system carries a permanent regulatory record — for both the individual and the firm. Consumer Duty requires firms to act to deliver good outcomes; the absence of an accountable human in the loop is direct evidence of failure to act.

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: DUAA 2025 Article 22A, in force since 5 February 2026, provides the statutory definition: a decision is 'based solely on automated processing' only where there is no genuine or meaningful human involvement. The ICO's Recruitment Rewired report (March 2026) defines what 'meaningful' requires in practice: the human reviewer must have real authority, discretion and competence to alter the decision before it is applied. A nominal reviewer who rubber-stamps automated outputs does not meet this standard — the ICO is explicit that this will be treated as solely automated regardless of whether a person nominally sits in the chain. Article 22C mandates that employers provide candidates with the right to human review. That right requires a named individual who can genuinely exercise it. Without a named accountable individual with a functioning override mechanism, the employer cannot comply with Article 22C — the mandatory safeguard is structurally absent. In an Employment Tribunal discrimination claim, 'the AI decided' is not a defence: the Equality Act places liability on the employer for discriminatory outcomes regardless of whether the tool was internally developed or procured from a third party. A named individual with oversight capability is both the legal requirement and the only mechanism by which that liability can be actively managed.
sector_risk.legal: The SRA has confirmed in its published compliance guidance that COLPs are expected to be responsible for regulatory compliance when new technology is introduced (SRA Innovate: Compliance tips for solicitors). The COLP's duties under SRA Code Rule 9.1 — take all reasonable steps to ensure compliance by the firm and its managers, employees and those it contracts with — extend to every AI tool in use across the practice. Where no named individual has oversight of a specific AI deployment and no override mechanism exists, the COLP cannot discharge those duties for that system. In Ayinde v London Borough of Hackney (May 2025), the court was explicit: a solicitor's duty to the court applies regardless of whether AI was used to assist with the work. The reliance on AI-generated content without meaningful human oversight was a breach of professional duties. That judgment establishes that named individual accountability — a solicitor who can demonstrate they reviewed, understood and approved each AI-assisted output — is the professional standard. A firm where no named individual oversees an AI deployment has no mechanism to evidence that standard was met for any matter the system touched.
sector_risk.retail: Retail AI systems making consumer-facing decisions — pricing, promotion, product recommendations, customer communications — require a named individual who can intervene and override. The CMA's AI principles require that algorithmic systems are subject to human oversight and that accountability is assigned. Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, a retailer is liable for automated commitments made through its systems — and without a named individual with override capability, there is no mechanism to prevent harmful or incorrect automated commitments from executing. Where consumer credit or financial promotions are AI-influenced, FCA oversight of embedded finance and BNPL products means accountability is a regulatory requirement, not just best practice.

risk_full.regulatory: EU AI Act human oversight requirements for high-risk systems (Art. 14) require that natural persons can oversee, intervene in, and override automated systems. No override mechanism means this requirement is not met.
risk_full.operational: Personal liability exposure for accountable individuals is unmitigated. In the event of a harmful decision, there is no record of oversight.
risk_full.reputational: Board-level governance failure if an incident occurs. Senior leadership accountability is established by law; the absence of oversight mechanisms makes it impossible to demonstrate it was exercised.

NHS England's AI governance policy requires organisations to demonstrate a structured path to compliance — not just awareness of gaps.

NHS Trusts operating multiple ungoverned AI systems face compounding risk — a single incident triggers investigation of all systems, not just the one involved.
healthcare.reputational: A pattern of DCB0160 non-compliance identified in CQC inspection, with no evidence of a remediation plan, is the worst possible posture in a serious incident investigation. financial_services.regulatory: The FCA's position is explicit: firms that wait for AI-specific rules before acting on governance gaps will find themselves behind both their peers and their supervisors. The Treasury Committee's January 2026 report warned that political patience for inaction has limits. A pattern of unaddressed AI governance gaps with no remediation roadmap is the posture most likely to attract supervisory intervention under existing FCA Principles 2 and 3.
financial_services.operational: Each new agentic deployment without a governance architecture adds to the firm's cumulative SM&CR exposure. Senior Managers accountable for ungoverned AI systems face personal liability that compounds with each deployment. A firm deploying AI at speed without governance is accelerating its own enforcement risk.
financial_services.reputational: FCA enforcement actions citing systemic governance failure — not a single incident but a pattern — are public and permanent. A firm that cannot demonstrate a remediation roadmap when the FCA asks has no defence. The Consumer Duty framing makes this worse: the question is not whether the firm knew, but whether it acted.

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: The ICO has moved from guidance to active enforcement posture on automated recruitment decisions. Its March 2026 Recruitment Rewired report is explicitly a call to action — the ICO has already engaged over 30 employers, written to 16 organisations requiring improved practices, and stated that enforcement action will follow for those that fall short. The ADM and profiling guidance consultation runs until 29 May 2026, after which a statutory code of practice will follow. An organisation with multiple recruitment AI governance gaps and no remediation roadmap will face a defined compliance gap on the day that code is published — with no evidence of steps taken to close it. The House of Commons Business and Trade Committee closed its inquiry on 3 April 2026; its findings will add political pressure on the ICO to enforce. The Equality and Human Rights Commission is concurrently scrutinising discriminatory AI systems, meaning an organisation with unaddressed AI governance gaps may face attention from two regulators simultaneously. An organisation that cannot produce a remediation roadmap — even a one-page plan with dated milestones — when either regulator asks is in the worst possible evidential position.
sector_risk.legal: The SRA's risk outlook identifies law firms without AI governance frameworks as the primary enforcement risk in the sector. With 89% of UK legal professionals now using AI tools (Clio UK and Ireland Legal Insights Report 2026) and only approximately 10% of firms having formal governance policies (Thomson Reuters, 2024), the gap between adoption and accountability is at its widest point. The Law Society's AI governance guidance (May 2025) is explicit: governance cannot be retrofitted after adoption. A firm that has deployed AI across fee earner work without governance infrastructure cannot close that gap retrospectively — it can only establish a roadmap for remediation from this point forward. Under SRA Code Rule 2.5, the firm has an ongoing obligation to identify, monitor and manage material risks to the business. Where AI governance gaps have been identified — whether through a CLEARANCE engagement, internal review, or client complaint — and no remediation roadmap has been produced, the firm is in breach of Rule 2.5. The 2025 High Court judgments in Ayinde v London Borough of Hackney and Gloriose Ndaryiyumvire v Birmingham City University demonstrate that courts treat AI governance failures as professional conduct failures. A firm with multiple structural governance gaps and no plan to close them has no credible defence when the next incident occurs — and no evidence that it took the SRA's risk signal seriously.
sector_risk.retail: A retailer with multiple AI governance gaps and no remediation roadmap faces compounding exposure across consumer protection, data privacy and emerging AI regulation. The CMA's pro-competition framework for digital markets is actively enforced, and algorithmic pricing and personalisation tools are under direct scrutiny. The Product Safety and Metrology Bill (2024) extends AI product liability principles into retail contexts. ICO enforcement on consumer-facing AI is increasing. A retailer that cannot demonstrate a structured path to governed AI — even a one-page roadmap with named owner and milestones — has no defensible posture when any of these regulators asks.

risk_full.operational: Each new agentic deployment without a governance architecture adds to cumulative exposure. Without a remediation path, the gap between deployment velocity and governance maturity widens.
risk_full.reputational: A documented pattern of governance failures without corrective action is the worst possible posture in a regulatory investigation or insurance claim. The absence of a plan is itself the evidence.

AI tools used to monitor productivity, screen communications, track location or analyse behaviour are processing special category data in many cases — triggering stricter obligations. An employer who cannot demonstrate a DPIA, a disclosed monitoring policy, and a documented necessity assessment has no governance foundation for any monitoring data used in employment decisions.

Article 22C, in force since 5 February 2026, requires employers to give employees the right to make representations about automated decisions and to request human review. Without a documented appeal mechanism, this mandatory safeguard is absent. Equality Act exposure is particularly acute: AI performance models trained on historical data risk encoding existing workforce disparities. An employer who cannot demonstrate how their performance AI was tested for bias and what the appeal route is has no defence to a discrimination claim based on AI-influenced assessment. The BTC inquiry examined algorithmic management specifically — this area is under active political and regulatory scrutiny.

Equality Act 2010 applies where AI scoring produces disparate outcomes across protected characteristics. evidenced_by: AI tools used in disciplinary investigations (HR intake confirms disciplinary AI)

Record of how AI outputs were used — what the tool produced, whether the adjudicator agreed with it, and any departures from AI recommendations

sector_risk.recruitment_hr: Any AI tool used in a disciplinary investigation — sentiment analysis of communications, pattern detection in attendance or productivity data, recommendation engines for sanction levels — must be documented in the disciplinary record alongside the human adjudicator's reasoning. The ACAS Code requires that the basis for any disciplinary decision is recorded and communicated to the employee. Where AI contributed to that basis and the contribution is undocumented, the employer cannot produce the record the Code requires. Employment tribunals have shown willingness to draw adverse inferences from incomplete disciplinary records — and the involvement of an unexplained AI tool makes the inference more likely, not less. The employer must be able to show that a named human adjudicator made the decision, understood the AI input, and exercised independent judgment.

Employment Tribunal unfair dismissal claims require the employer to demonstrate a fair reason and a fair procedure; absence of a contemporaneous decision record undermines both. LEG-G09-HALLUCINATION.name: AI-assisted legal drafting without hallucination controls

risk_score.rationale: HIGH likelihood because 89% of UK legal professionals use AI tools but verification protocols are rarely documented; HIGH impact because consequences span contempt of court, negligence, SRA investigation and client loss simultaneously

evidenced_by: AI tools used for drafting, research or content generation for client matters (legal intake)
No documented verification protocol requiring solicitor to check AI output

Training records — evidence that all fee earners using AI tools have been trained on verification requirements and the limitations of specific tools in use

sector_risk.legal: The SRA's published risk outlook on AI identifies hallucination risk as the primary technical failure mode in AI-assisted legal work. High Court judgments in 2025 — including Ayinde v London Borough of Hackney — demonstrated that courts will impose wasted costs orders and consider SRA referrals where AI-generated inaccuracies reach submissions. The Law Society's guidance is explicit: solicitors must take positive steps to ensure that any information submitted to court is accurate and from genuine, verifiable sources. This is not discharged by general vigilance — it requires a structural protocol: every citation verified against primary source, every statutory reference checked against current legislation, every AI-generated proposition reviewed by the supervising solicitor before delivery. Without a documented verification protocol, the firm has no evidence that this standard was applied to any matter, and no defence when an error is found. The Clio 2026 Legal Insights Report found 89% of UK legal professionals use AI — the verification gap affects the entire profession.
sector_risk.retail: This gap applies to retail organisations only where the specific AI deployment falls within a regulated HR, legal or financial services function (e.g. embedded BNPL, regulated insurance products, legal compliance tooling). Submitting AI-generated content containing inaccuracies — even without intent to deceive — breaches these obligations. sector_risk.legal: AI tools used to generate legal advice — research summaries, opinion drafts, risk assessments, contract analyses — are now widespread across UK law firms. A supervision framework is not optional governance — it is the structural mechanism by which a firm can demonstrate that every piece of AI-assisted advice was reviewed by a qualified solicitor before delivery. Without it, the firm cannot distinguish supervised from unsupervised advice output in any client file, cannot evidence competence under SRA Code Rule 4.2, and cannot demonstrate to professional indemnity insurers that AI use is controlled. A supervision framework requires three things: a named reviewer for each matter type using AI advice tools, a defined review standard (what the reviewer must check and to what depth), and a file notation confirming the review was completed. These are low-cost controls with high-value defensive output.

sector_risk.legal: The SRA's risk outlook specifically identifies AI tools processing client data without proper controls as a primary governance risk. The obligation is clear: before any client data enters an AI tool, the firm must have a Data Processing Agreement with the vendor, confirmed that client data is not used for model training, and verified the vendor's retention and deletion policies. In practice, many firms are using consumer-grade AI tools — where these controls either do not exist or require active opt-out — for client work. A single matter where client instructions entered a tool that retained them or used them for training is a confidentiality breach. There is no de minimis threshold: the SRA Code treats confidentiality as an absolute obligation. A confidentiality control framework — a register of approved AI tools, DPAs for each, and a rule that unapproved tools cannot be used with client data — is the minimum required governance.

Keeping AI training data, decision logs or monitoring data without a defined end date is a storage limitation breach. The ICO has specifically targeted AI recruitment tools for retaining candidate data without retention limits.
healthcare.operational: Keeping more data than necessary makes any data breach worse — more people affected, higher fines. It also makes responding to deletion requests very difficult if the data is spread across AI systems with no retention controls.
healthcare.reputational: ICO enforcement for retention failures in AI contexts — particularly in recruitment and HR — is on the public register. Discovery of indefinitely retained candidate or employee AI data is an employment brand and regulatory credibility issue.

Failure to respond to a subject access request within one month is a direct ICO enforcement trigger — and the ICO has confirmed this is a 2025/26 priority.

healthcare.reputational: ICO enforcement actions for failure to respond to data subject requests are on the public record. In HR and legal contexts, the affected individuals are employees or clients. Both carry significant reputational weight.

healthcare.regulatory: UK GDPR requires a Data Processing Agreement before any vendor handles personal data on your behalf. Without one, the processing is unlawful. The organisation remains liable as controller for any breach by its AI vendors — including training data misuse and retention failures.
healthcare.operational: Without a DPA, there are no contractual rights over what the vendor does with the data. No right to audit. No right to require deletion. No indemnity if they cause a breach. If the vendor misuses the data, the organisation has no basis for remedy.
healthcare.reputational: A breach by an AI vendor processing client or employee data without a DPA creates joint liability — and the organisation cannot show it took reasonable steps to protect the data. In legal contexts, client confidentiality obligations make this a serious professional conduct matter.
